newsitem.title: GERMANY: Leaders say German steel merger talks faring well.
newsitem.headline: Leaders say German steel merger talks faring well.

text.p: German political and economic leaders said on Sunday prospects for a peaceful end to German steel group Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp's hostile takeover bid for rival Thyssen AG appeared to be improving.

But tension remained as Thyssen's works council called for a massive protest on Tuesday in Frankfurt's financial quarter and weekend media reported that Krupp was likely to resume its takeover bid as early as the first week of April.

Thyssen chief executive Dieter Vogel said talks between the two groups were on "a good path" and could reach a conclusion as soon as Wednesday -- a day before Krupp's deadline to reach a deal to avert a full-blown takeover bid.

Vogel participated in the secret weekend talks with Krupp chief executive Gerhard Cromme and their steel unit executives under the guidance of former Mercedes Benz AG chief executive Helmut Werner, who was called in to mediate in the dispute.

The talks, described by one source as taking place in a "good climate", have focused on ways to integrate the steel units under the majority control of Thyssen, which employs about 20,000 workers in the unit that has annual revenues of about 10 billion marks ($5.9 billion) -- about twice the size of Krupp's unit.
The talks, which began on Thursday, were sparked by Krupp's rare bid for the larger Thyssen earlier last week that shocked Germany's informal code against hostile takeovers.

A merger between Krupp and Thyssen steel units would create one of the industry's largest groups. But Krupp has said a full merger of the two companies would create cost savings in other areas as well, such as engineering and automotive components.

Thyssen's works council called on some 50,000 workers to stage a protest on Tuesday in Frankfurt, the nation's financial capital, as top politicans, including Chancellor Helmut Kohl, called on both companies to show social responsibility.

"We are going to Frankfurt because we fear that our future cannot be helped by the democratically-elected government in Bonn but will instead be decided by the banks," said Thyssen works council leader Georg Bongen in announcing the rally.

The takeover attempt has sparked spontaneous work stoppages by thousands of steel workers in the Ruhr valley heartland and local politicians intervened, persuading the two companies to begin the talks over a merger of just their steel companies.

Despite expectations of ongoing labour unrest, Wolfgang Clement, the economics minister in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia where the two groups are based, said on Sunday that he expected a co-operation deal to be reached.

Clement's views were echoed by Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry, who said he too believed Krupp and Thyssen would find a way to unify their steel operations to remain competitive but avoid massive job losses.
"I would say a merger would be good for both companies, particularly in the long-term," Henkel told German television network ZDF in an interview programme along with Clement.

Clement, a member of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), said he had the "impression that these talks have been very constructive I do not think the differences are dramatic. I want to see a merger in the end and not a hostile takeover."
But Die Welt newspaper said on Saturday that Krupp plans to relaunch its hostile takeover bid as early as next week.
Citing reliable sources, the newspaper said Krupp believed Thyssen only agreed to the merger talks in order to win time.

Germany's Der Spiegel magazine also said at the weekend that studies by Deutsche Bank AG , Dresdner Bank AG and investment bank Goldman Sachs showed a merger could show positive results as early as spring 1998.
The study, done at a cost of over 200 million marks for Krupp, assumed both companies could sell off a number of units and that Krupp could repay the takeover debts by the year 2000.

Focus news magazine said a top Deutsche Bank AG official did not rule out resigning from the Thyssen supervisory board after trade unions sharply criticised Deutsche and Dresdner for their role in the takeover bid.

"I will not rule out that I will give up my mandate at the end of the meeting (on Thursday)," Ulrich Cartellieri, who represents Deutsche's shareholder interests on the Thyssen board, said in an interview released ahead of publication on Monday.
